name: Judaism
line: Give thanks, study with a friend, do justice and keep one day holy.

quote.text: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.

quotes.text: If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when?
It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it.
Only to do justice, and to love goodness, and to walk modestly with your God.
Whoever saves a single life, it is as if he had saved an entire world.
The seventh day is a palace in time which we build.

words.usage: The five books of Moses, and more widely the whole body of Jewish teaching, written and oral.
One of the 613 obligations of the Torah. In everyday speech, any good deed.
The seventh day, from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall: rest, prayer, three meals and no work.
Hello, goodbye and the name of the hope. From a root meaning complete.

words.meaning: Justice; giving to those in need
words.usage: Usually translated charity, but the root means justice. Giving is an obligation, owed even by the poor.
Loyal, generous love shown in acts: visiting the sick, welcoming guests, burying the dead.
From mystical teaching about gathering scattered sparks. Now also the duty to work for a more just society.
Turning back to the right path. It requires admitting the wrong, making amends and not repeating it.
Three daily services. The Hebrew verb to pray is reflexive: it also means to judge oneself.
The inner attention that turns a recited prayer or a routine act into a real one.
A short formula of thanks said before eating, on seeing a rainbow, on hearing good or bad news. Tradition asks for a hundred a day.

words.meaning: The way to walk; Jewish law
words.usage: The detailed practice that shapes eating, work, rest, business and family life.
The vast record of rabbinic debate, completed in Babylonia around the sixth century. It preserves the losing arguments too.
Stories and readings that fill the gaps in the biblical text and draw new meaning from it.
Two people reading a text aloud and arguing over it. The classic way of Jewish learning.
An argument for the sake of heaven is one conducted to find the truth, and it is prized.
Food permitted by the dietary laws: no pork or shellfish, meat and milk kept apart, animals slaughtered with care.
The ten adults needed for public prayer. Some things cannot be done alone.
The declaration of God’s oneness from Deuteronomy, said morning and night and as the last words of life.
A small case on the doorframe holding the Shema, touched on entering and leaving.
From the word for order. It sets out the daily, Sabbath and festival services.
Said for a parent for eleven months and on each anniversary. It praises God and never mentions death.
The week of mourning at home after a burial, when the community comes to sit with the bereaved and bring food.
A wedding or a coming of age, and the duty to rejoice.
The toast. Life is the value that outweighs almost every law.
The principle that nearly any commandment must be set aside to preserve life.
Harmful speech about another person, forbidden even when it is true.
From Genesis: every human being is made so. The ground of equal dignity.
Someone decent, responsible and kind. The highest ordinary compliment.
A scholar ordained to teach and to decide questions of law. Not a priest. Any knowledgeable Jew can lead prayers.

practices.name: Waking with thanks
practices.instructions: Before you get out of bed and before you reach for anything, say thank you for waking up. The traditional words are: I give thanks before you, living and enduring King, that you have returned my soul to me in compassion; great is your faithfulness. Say them, or your own words, for a moment. Then get up. The rule of this Onda is to give thanks before you take.
practices.why: Modeh ani is the first thing a Jewish child learns to say each morning. It makes the day begin with gratitude rather than demand.
variations: Say it in Hebrew, phonetically.
Say it with a hand on the heart.
Add one thing you are grateful for today.

practices.name: Wash the hands, wake the day
practices.instructions: Wash your hands slowly on getting up, pouring water over each in turn. Some Jews keep a cup and bowl by the bed for this. Take it as a pause before the day begins, an act of readiness. Dry them while thinking: I am ready for a good day. Netilat yadayim is the traditional name.
practices.why: Washing the hands on waking is a Jewish custom, a bridge from sleep to day. A guest can borrow it as a small reset.
variations: Use a cup and pour three times.
Wash with a prayer of thanks.
Dry your hands thoughtfully.

practices.name: One saying of the fathers
practices.instructions: Read one saying from Pirkei Avot, Ethics of the Fathers, with your morning tea. Read it twice. Ask what it says, what it could mean and how it might apply today. Write it on a card and keep it in your pocket. Work through the book across the weeks. A good start is: who is wise? One who learns from everyone.
practices.why: Pirkei Avot is a short collection of rabbinic sayings on conduct, studied for about 1,800 years. It is practical, witty and wise, and each saying stands alone.
variations: Read it aloud to someone at the table.
Compare two translations.
Argue with one saying in your notebook.

practices.name: Guard your tongue
practices.instructions: Until noon, say nothing about people who are not present that you would not say in front of them. Notice every impulse to gossip, joke at someone’s cost or pass on a rumour. Lashon hara, evil speech, is a serious matter in Jewish ethics. Catch the impulse, drop it and say something kind or nothing.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to guard your tongue. Jewish teachers regard careless speech as one of the gravest harms, because it cannot be taken back.
variations: Extend it to the whole day.
Count your slips.
Praise someone who is not present.

practices.name: A mitzvah for today
practices.instructions: Choose one good deed for today, a mitzvah, and write it on a card: visit a sick friend, return a lost item, help a neighbour, feed someone. A mitzvah is a good deed and a commandment at once. Put the card where you will see it. At night, check it off and feel the small pleasure of having done it.
practices.why: The word mitzvah is used in everyday speech for any good deed. Choosing one in the morning ensures that it happens.
variations: Choose a mitzvah between you and a family member.
Do two good deeds instead of one.
Do one you would rather not.

practices.name: A Hebrew word a day
practices.instructions: Learn one Hebrew word today and use it three times. Start with shalom, peace, hello and goodbye; toda, thank you; b’vakasha, please; tov, good; chaver, friend. Say it aloud, write it on your hand and use it with someone. Hebrew was a language of prayer and study for centuries and is spoken today as a living language.
practices.why: Hebrew has been revived as a spoken language in the last century, after thousands of years of prayer and text. A single word a day builds a feeling for it.
variations: Learn the Hebrew letters one by one.
Write the word in Hebrew script.
Teach the word to a child.

practices.name: A blessing before you eat
practices.instructions: Do not put anything in your mouth today without stopping first. Look at the food. Think where it came from: earth, tree, vine, someone’s work. Say a sentence of thanks, in the traditional form or your own, such as blessed are you who brings forth bread from the earth. Then eat. Do this for every bite or drink you take, even a biscuit.
practices.why: Jewish tradition has a blessing for nearly every food and experience. Giving thanks before taking is the first rule of this Onda.
variations: Say it aloud, however quietly.
Say the blessing and give a bit to someone.
Bless a drink as well.

practices.name: Study with a partner
practices.instructions: Find one person to study with for the length of the Onda, in person or by phone. Take a short text, a few lines only: start with Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers. Read it aloud. Ask what it says, what it could mean and where you disagree. Argue and listen. The aim is not to agree but to learn together.
practices.why: Havruta, paired study, is the heart of Jewish learning. Two people with one text and plenty of questions is how it has been done for centuries.
variations: Study by video call.
Study a short story instead.
Take turns choosing the text.

practices.name: Visit or call someone alone
practices.instructions: Call or visit someone who is ill, lonely or housebound. Bikur cholim, visiting the sick, is one of the great acts of kindness in Jewish tradition. Bring a small thing: soup, a book, flowers or just your time. Ask how they are and listen. Stay for the time they can take, and leave them lighter.
practices.why: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah that Jewish teachers say brings healing to the visitor too. It makes no demand but your presence.
variations: Bring a meal.
Read aloud to them.
Call someone who has no visitors.

practices.name: Argue for the sake of heaven
practices.instructions: Find a friend to argue with about a question that matters, in the manner of the rabbis. State your case, listen to theirs and keep your temper. A machloket, a disagreement, for the sake of heaven, is one in which both sides want the truth and not the victory. Finish by saying what you learned from the other.
practices.why: Pirkei Avot praises arguments for the sake of heaven, like those of Hillel and Shammai, and says they last. A good argument is a form of respect.
variations: Argue a question the other way round.
Argue about a text.
End with a hug.

practices.name: Ask a good question
practices.instructions: Ask one real question today, one you do not know the answer to, of someone who may know. Listen to the whole answer and ask a follow-up. The story goes that the physicist Isidor Rabi’s mother asked him each day after school, not what did you learn but did you ask a good question today? Write down your question and its answer.
practices.why: Questioning is prized in Jewish learning, from the Passover seder’s four questions onwards. A good question is as valuable as a good answer.
variations: Ask a child what they wondered.
Ask a question you are afraid to ask.
Keep a list of questions.

practices.name: Repair what you break
practices.instructions: Fix something today that you broke or neglected: an object, a promise, a friendship, a debt. Do it properly and without excuses. Tikkun, repair, is a theme running through Jewish thought, from fixing a chair to mending the world. The rule of this Onda is to repair what you break.
practices.why: Tikkun olam, repairing the world, starts with small, personal repairs. Mending what you broke is the nearest place to begin.
variations: Apologise and mend something material.
Return what you borrowed.
Repair something for a neighbour.

practices.name: Tzedakah before sunset
practices.instructions: Keep a jar, a box or a dedicated account. Every day before the sun goes down put something in, however small. On Friday afternoon add a little more. At the end of each week give what has gathered to someone who needs it or to an organisation you trust. Say, as you drop the coin: for justice. The rule of this Onda is to give something every day.
practices.why: Tzedakah, usually translated as charity, means justice or righteousness. Giving is treated as an obligation, even for the poor, and a daily coin keeps it habitual.
variations: Give to a person, not just a charity.
Let a child choose where it goes.
Make the jar beautiful.

practices.name: Forgiving before sleep
practices.instructions: At the end of the day take stock. What did I do well? Where did I fall short, and toward whom? What will I repair tomorrow, and how? Then say, and mean as far as you can: I forgive anyone who angered or wronged me today. Let it go before you sleep. If it is too soon, say that you are trying.
practices.why: The bedtime prayer in the Jewish liturgy includes forgiving anyone who angered you. A daily accounting of the soul, cheshbon hanefesh, keeps the heart light.
variations: Write the three questions in a notebook.
Forgive one person by name.
Say sorry to someone in the morning.

practices.name: A candle pause
practices.instructions: On any evening, light two candles in a safe place and sit with them for ten minutes. Cover your eyes for a moment, then open them to the light, as the Friday candle-lighter does. Say what you are thankful for. Switch off screens during the ten minutes. Let the lights mark the edge between the working day and the evening.
practices.why: Lighting candles marks the beginning of Shabbat in Jewish homes. A borrowed candle pause gives any evening a gentle border.
variations: Light them on Friday evening.
Add a pause for a family hug.
Put them on a table with flowers.

practices.name: Sing a niggun
practices.instructions: Sing a niggun, a wordless melody, such as the Hasidim sing. Pick a simple tune with a repeated phrase and sing it with ya-ba-bam or lai-lai-lai, over and over, getting louder and quieter. Sing alone or with someone. A niggun carries feeling words cannot. Let it grow until it feels right to stop.
practices.why: Hasidic communities sing niggunim to lift the heart without words. They are easy to join, joyful and soothing.
variations: Look up a recording and sing along.
Sing it while washing up.
Make up your own niggun.

practices.name: A tale of the Hasidim
practices.instructions: Read or tell a short story from Martin Buber’s Tales of the Hasidim, or one by I. B. Singer or Sholem Aleichem. Choose something with a twist and a moral, like the rabbi who found God at the bottom of a well. Read it aloud. The stories are brief and have been told at the table for generations.
practices.why: Hasidic and Yiddish tales are a treasure of Jewish storytelling. They are short, funny and wise, and good at bedtime.
variations: Tell it to a child.
Read a story by Isaac Bashevis Singer.
Retell it with a modern setting.

practices.name: A little Shabbat hour
practices.instructions: Take one hour of the evening and make it a rest. No work, no errands, no shopping, no screens, no news. Eat something good, talk, read, nap, walk. Heschel called Shabbat a palace in time. One hour of it, borrowed, is a gift to yourself. The rule of this Onda is to keep one day apart; start with an hour.
practices.why: Shabbat is a weekly day of rest, and the idea that rest is holy is Judaism’s gift to the world. A short hour is a small taste.
variations: Do it on Friday evening.
Switch off the phone and hide it.
Invite someone to share it.

practices.name: Bake challah
practices.instructions: Bake a braided egg bread. Mix flour, yeast, warm water, eggs, oil, a little honey and salt, knead for ten minutes, let it rise until doubled, braid three strands and brush with egg. Bake until golden. Share the loaf with a neighbour or friend while still warm. Challah is baked for Shabbat and holidays all over the Jewish world.
practices.why: Baking challah is a loved Friday ritual in Jewish homes. The smell of the loaf in the oven fills the house with a sense of occasion.
variations: Braid a round loaf for the new year.
Add raisins.
Bake two and give one away.

practices.name: A Friday-style supper
practices.instructions: Hold a Friday-style supper with a guest or two. Light two candles, put out bread and a cup of grape juice, and say thank you for the week. Eat slowly, with songs, stories and questions at the table. Leave the phones in another room. Invite someone who would otherwise be alone. Make the meal last long.
practices.why: The Shabbat table is the centre of Jewish family life: bread, wine or juice, song and talk. Inviting a guest is one of its greatest pleasures.
variations: Ask each guest to bring a story.
Sing a niggun after the meal.
Go for a walk afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Pirkei Avot
immersePlan.text: Read one chapter of the Ethics of the Fathers. Choose the saying you most disagree with and argue with it in writing.

immersePlan.name: Read a few pages of Heschel’s The Sabbath
immersePlan.text: Read a short stretch of Abraham Joshua Heschel’s lyrical essay on time and rest. Underline one sentence.

immersePlan.name: Read a Hasidic tale
immersePlan.text: Read three or four short stories from Martin Buber’s collection of Hasidic tales. Tell your favourite to someone later.

immersePlan.name: Watch Fiddler on the Roof
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1971 musical about Tevye the milkman, his daughters and a changing world. Sing along to Tradition, If I Were a Rich Man and Sunrise, Sunset.

immersePlan.name: Watch Ushpizin
immersePlan.text: Watch Gidi Dar’s 2004 comedy about a Jerusalem couple whose Sukkot guests turn out to be rather more than they bargained for. It is warm and funny.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Shtisel
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of the Israeli series about an ultra-Orthodox family in Jerusalem. Notice the conversations around the table.

immersePlan.name: Listen to klezmer
immersePlan.text: Play klezmer, the music of Eastern European Jewish celebrations: clarinet, violin and accordion that laugh and cry. Dance in your chair.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Ladino songs
immersePlan.text: Play songs in the old Spanish of the Sephardic Jews, sung by Flory Jagoda or Yasmin Levy. Listen for the sadness and the sweetness.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Who by Fire
immersePlan.text: Play Leonard Cohen’s song based on a prayer for the Day of Atonement. Listen to the list of ways the year could end, and to his soft voice.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Sarajevo Haggadah
immersePlan.text: Look at the illuminated Passover book made in Spain around 1350 that survived the Inquisition and the Bosnian war. Choose a page.

immersePlan.name: Look at Chagall’s Jerusalem Windows
immersePlan.text: Look at Marc Chagall’s twelve stained-glass windows, one for each tribe, in deep blues, reds and golds. Choose your tribe by colour.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Dura-Europos murals
immersePlan.text: Look at the third-century wall paintings of Bible scenes from a synagogue in Syria, buried under a rampart before the city fell. Find the baby Moses.

immersePlan.name: Eat challah
immersePlan.text: Eat a warm, braided egg bread, with butter or honey. Tear it rather than cut it, and share the first piece.

immersePlan.name: Make chicken soup with matzah balls
immersePlan.text: Simmer chicken with onion, carrot and dill for an hour and drop in dumplings of matzah meal. The remedy of Jewish grandmothers. Serve a bowl to someone who needs it.

immersePlan.name: Cook shakshuka
immersePlan.text: Poach eggs in a pan of spiced tomato and pepper sauce with cumin and paprika. Eat it straight from the pan with bread.

immersePlan.name: Pour a cup of grape juice
immersePlan.text: Fill a cup to the brim with grape juice and hold it up before drinking, as on Friday evening, saying thank you for the week.

immersePlan.name: Drink tea with lemon in a glass
immersePlan.text: Brew strong black tea and serve it in a glass with a slice of lemon, sipped through a sugar lump if you like. A drink of Eastern Europe.

immersePlan.name: Drink mint tea
immersePlan.text: Pour hot water on fresh mint and a bit of green tea and sweeten to taste. It is the afternoon drink of Jews from North Africa.

immersePlan.name: Light two candles
immersePlan.text: Light two candles on Friday evening, or tonight, and sit for a moment. Cover your eyes, then open them to the flame.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the mezuzah
immersePlan.text: Read about the small case on the right doorpost of a Jewish home, with a scroll inside. Notice them next time you pass a Jewish home.

immersePlan.name: Learn about stones on a grave
immersePlan.text: Read why visitors leave small stones on Jewish graves, not flowers. Then visit a grave of someone you have lost and leave a stone.

immersePlan.name: Play dreidel
immersePlan.text: Spin the four-sided top with a friend and play for chocolate coins. Each letter tells you whether to take, give or put in.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of chess
immersePlan.text: Play a game of chess. Jewish communities have loved the game for a thousand years and produced many world champions. Play a friend.

immersePlan.name: Play The Shivah
immersePlan.text: Play the short detective game in which a rabbi in Manhattan becomes involved in a death. It is thoughtful and funny.

immersePlan.name: Mark Hanukkah
immersePlan.text: Hanukkah comes in December and lasts eight nights. Light a candle each evening, eat something fried and play dreidel.

immersePlan.name: Look up Passover
immersePlan.text: Read about the seder, the meal in which the story of leaving Egypt is told with questions, food and song. Ask a question at dinner.

immersePlan.name: Look up Sukkot
immersePlan.text: Sukkot is the autumn harvest festival in which families eat in a hut open to the sky. Eat one meal outside under a roof of branches.

immersePlan.name: Practise tikkun olam
immersePlan.text: Tikkun olam is repairing the world. Make one small repair today, in an object, a relationship or a place.

immersePlan.name: Practise chesed
immersePlan.text: Chesed is loving-kindness. Do one kindness today that nobody expects and that you cannot be repaid for.

immersePlan.name: Be a mensch
immersePlan.text: Mensch is a Yiddish word for a decent, upright person. Do the right thing in one situation today when nobody would know.

rules.why: On waking and before every meal. Say it in words.
No gossip and no talking a person down, even if every word is true.
Money, food or time, before sunset. It is justice, and it is owed.
A page, a paragraph, a verse, with a partner if you can. Ask why.
One day in seven without work, purchases or screens, with good food and people.
When you wrong someone, go to them, say so and make it good. Do it within the week.

read.title: Pirkei Avot: Ethics of the Fathers
read.creator: The Mishnah; many translations
read.why: Six short chapters of sayings from the early rabbis. The usual first text for study, and free in every prayer book and online.

read.title: The Sabbath
read.creator: Abraham Joshua Heschel
read.why: A hundred pages on why Judaism builds its cathedrals in time and not in space. Beautiful and brief.

read.title: Tanakh: The Holy Scriptures
read.creator: Jewish Publication Society translation
read.why: The Hebrew Bible in the standard modern Jewish translation. Begin with Genesis, Exodus, Ruth and Ecclesiastes.

read.title: Jewish Literacy
read.creator: Joseph Telushkin
read.why: Some 350 two-page entries on everything from Abraham to Yiddish. A good book to dip into.

read.title: The Chosen
read.creator: Chaim Potok
read.why: Two boys in 1940s Brooklyn, one Hasidic and one modern Orthodox, become friends over a baseball injury and the Talmud.

read.title: Tales of the Hasidim
read.creator: Martin Buber
read.why: Hundreds of short stories about the early Hasidic masters. Each takes a minute to read and a week to digest.

watch.title: Fiddler on the Roof
watch.creator: Norman Jewison
watch.why: A milkman in a Russian village in 1905 argues with God while tradition slips through his fingers. The musical the whole world knows.

watch.title: Ushpizin
watch.creator: Gidi Dar
watch.why: A poor, devout couple in Jerusalem receive unexpected guests for the festival of Sukkot. Made with and by members of the ultra-Orthodox community.

watch.title: Shtisel
watch.creator: Ori Elon and Yehonatan Indursky
watch.why: A television drama about a strictly Orthodox family in Jerusalem. Tender, funny and never condescending.

watch.title: A Serious Man
watch.creator: Joel and Ethan Coen
watch.why: A physics professor in 1960s Minnesota watches his life collapse and seeks advice from three rabbis. The Book of Job as dark comedy.

listen.title: Kol Nidre
listen.creator: Cantorial tradition; Max Bruch’s setting for cello, 1880
listen.why: The declaration sung three times at dusk as the Day of Atonement begins. Hear a cantor sing it, then hear the cello.

listen.title: Klezmer
listen.creator: The Klezmatics, Giora Feidman, Dave Tarras
listen.why: The wedding music of Eastern European Jews: a clarinet that laughs and cries.

listen.title: Who by Fire
listen.creator: Leonard Cohen
listen.why: A song built on the prayer Unetaneh Tokef, which asks on the New Year who will live and who will die.

listen.title: Ladino songs
listen.creator: Flory Jagoda, Yasmin Levy
listen.why: Songs in the Judeo-Spanish that the Jews expelled from Spain carried across the Mediterranean.

art.title: The Sarajevo Haggadah
art.creator: Scribes and painters of Catalonia
art.why: An illuminated Passover book, wine-stained from use. It left Spain with the expulsion, and was hidden from the Nazis by a Muslim librarian and from shelling in the 1990s.

art.title: The Dura-Europos synagogue murals
art.creator: Syria
art.why: Walls covered with scenes from the Bible, buried for seventeen centuries. They overturned the idea that ancient Jews made no pictures.

art.title: The Jerusalem Windows
art.creator: Marc Chagall; Hadassah Medical Centre, Jerusalem
art.why: Twelve stained-glass windows for the twelve tribes, in blazing colour with animals, fish and candlesticks and no human figures.

art.title: The Old-New Synagogue
art.creator: Prague, Czech Republic
art.why: The oldest working synagogue in Europe: a small Gothic hall with a banner given by an emperor. Legend puts the golem in its attic.

eat.title: Challah
eat.creator: Braided egg bread
eat.why: Two loaves on the Sabbath table, covered with a cloth, blessed, torn and dipped in salt.

eat.title: Chicken soup with matzah balls
eat.creator: Clear broth with dumplings of matzah meal
eat.why: The Ashkenazi cure for everything, served on Friday nights and at Passover.

eat.title: Cholent or hamin
eat.creator: Beans, barley, potatoes and meat cooked overnight
eat.why: Since cooking is not done on the Sabbath, a stew is started on Friday and left on low heat until Saturday lunch. Every community has a version.

eat.title: Shakshuka
eat.creator: Eggs poached in spiced tomato and pepper sauce
eat.why: Brought to Israel by Jews from North Africa and now eaten everywhere.

drink.title: Wine or grape juice for kiddush
drink.creator: A full cup
drink.why: The Sabbath and every festival begin with a blessing over wine. Grape juice is equally valid.

drink.title: Tea with lemon in a glass
drink.creator: Strong black tea
drink.why: The Russian Jewish habit, drunk through a sugar cube during study and argument.

drink.title: Mint tea
drink.creator: Green tea with fresh mint and sugar
drink.why: The drink of Moroccan Jewish hospitality.

customs.title: Lighting two candles
customs.creator: Friday, eighteen minutes before sunset
customs.why: The Sabbath is welcomed with light, usually by the woman of the house, who covers her eyes and says the blessing.

customs.title: The mezuzah
customs.creator: On the right doorpost
customs.why: A scroll in a case, set at an angle. People touch it and then kiss their fingers as they pass.

customs.title: Covering the head
customs.creator: The kippah
customs.why: A small cap worn by men, and in liberal communities by some women, as a sign of reverence. Visitors to a synagogue are usually offered one.

customs.title: Stones on a grave
customs.creator: A visit recorded
customs.why: Visitors leave a small stone on the headstone, not flowers. It shows that someone came and remembers.

games.title: Dreidel
games.creator: Spinning top game · Ashkenazi tradition
games.why: A four-sided top with Hebrew letters, played for nuts or chocolate coins at Hanukkah. The letters stand for: a great miracle happened there.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game
games.why: Loved in Jewish communities since the Middle Ages, when rabbis wrote poems about it. Steinitz, Lasker, Botvinnik, Tal and Judit Polgar came from Jewish families.

games.title: The Shivah
games.creator: Video game · Wadjet Eye Games
games.why: A point-and-click mystery in which a disillusioned New York rabbi investigates a death in his congregation. You can answer questions with questions.

festivals.title: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
festivals.creator: September or October
festivals.why: The New Year and, ten days later, the Day of Atonement: a twenty-five hour fast spent in prayer. Before it, people ask each other’s forgiveness.

festivals.title: Passover (Pesach)
festivals.creator: March or April, seven or eight days
festivals.why: The exodus from Egypt, retold at a home meal, the seder, built round questions asked by the youngest child. No leavened bread is eaten.

festivals.title: Sukkot
festivals.creator: September or October, a week
festivals.why: Families eat, and some sleep, in a hut roofed with branches through which the stars can be seen.

festivals.title: Hanukkah
festivals.creator: December, eight nights
festivals.why: One more candle is lit each evening to recall the rededication of the Temple. Fried food, songs and the dreidel.

places.title: The Western Wall
places.creator: Jerusalem
places.why: The surviving retaining wall of the Second Temple mount, where prayers have been said for centuries and notes are pressed between the stones. Dress modestly. Men and women pray in separate sections.

places.title: The Jewish Quarter (Josefov)
places.creator: Prague, Czech Republic
places.why: Six synagogues and an old cemetery with twelve thousand crowded headstones, including that of Rabbi Judah Loew.

places.title: The Portuguese Synagogue
places.creator: Amsterdam, Netherlands
places.why: Built in 1675 by descendants of Jews who fled Spain and Portugal. It is still lit only by candles.

places.title: Kazimierz and the POLIN Museum
places.creator: Kraków and Warsaw, Poland

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: Justice, justice shall you pursue, says Deuteronomy. The prophets judged a society by how it treated the widow, the orphan, the poor and the stranger.
ethics.practice: Find one unfair thing within your reach and do something about it.

ethics.title: Loving-kindness
ethics.text: The world is said to stand on three things: Torah, worship and acts of kindness. Kindness is practical: a meal, a visit, a lift, a loan.
ethics.practice: Visit, call or cook for someone who is ill or alone.

ethics.title: The stranger
ethics.text: You shall love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. The instruction appears, the rabbis counted, thirty-six times.
ethics.practice: Make one newcomer or outsider feel expected today.

ethics.title: Guarding speech
ethics.text: Words can kill a reputation, and the damage cannot be recalled. Gossip is said to harm three people: the speaker, the listener and the subject.
ethics.practice: Go a full day without discussing anyone who is not present.

ethics.title: Honouring parents
ethics.text: The fifth commandment. It means seeing that they have food, clothing and company, and not shaming them.
ethics.practice: Do something concrete for a parent or an elder this week.

ethics.title: Repentance and repair
ethics.text: For wrongs against another person, the Day of Atonement does not atone until you have gone to them and made it right.
ethics.practice: Make one overdue apology, with repair attached.

philosophy.title: One God, one humanity
philosophy.text: The Shema declares that God is one. From that follows a single moral law and a single human family, each member made in the divine image.
philosophy.practice: Treat the next person who annoys you as bearing that image.

philosophy.title: Covenant
philosophy.text: The relationship between God and Israel is a contract with obligations on both sides. One party may argue with the other. Abraham bargains over Sodom, and Job demands an answer.
philosophy.practice: Name the commitments you have chosen that now bind you. Are you keeping them?

philosophy.title: Deed over creed
philosophy.text: Judaism asks less what you believe than what you do. Holiness is built from many small acts repeated: what you eat, how you trade, when you stop.
philosophy.practice: Pick one value you hold and give it a fixed, daily action.

philosophy.title: Holiness in time
philosophy.text: The first thing the Bible calls holy is a day. The Sabbath makes a sanctuary out of hours, portable through every exile. For one day people stop making and simply are.
philosophy.practice: Decide when your day of rest begins and what stays outside it.

philosophy.title: The argument for the sake of heaven
philosophy.text: The Talmud records minority opinions with respect and often leaves disputes open. When the schools of Hillel and Shammai clashed, a voice said: both are the words of the living God.
philosophy.practice: In your next disagreement, state the other position so well that they would sign it.

philosophy.title: Repairing the world
philosophy.text: The sixteenth century mystic Isaac Luria taught that the vessels of creation shattered and that sparks of light lie scattered in everything. Each good act lifts one. The work is shared and unfinished.
philosophy.practice: Do one small, concrete repair today: mend something broken or mediate between two people.

philosophy.title: Choose life
philosophy.text: I have set before you life and death, says Deuteronomy: choose life. Saving life overrides almost every law. The tradition is stubbornly on the side of this world.
philosophy.practice: Say l’chaim to something today. Mark one good thing with a toast or a thank-you.

philosophy.title: Remember
philosophy.text: The command to remember appears again and again: the exodus, the Sabbath, what was done to you, that you were slaves. Memory is a duty, retold at the table so that it becomes each generation’s own.
philosophy.practice: Tell someone younger a story about where your family came from.

dayThemes: The whole Torah on one foot

intro: Judaism is the religion and way of life of the Jewish people. It is the oldest of the three great monotheisms and the root of the other two. There are about fifteen million Jews in the world today, nearly half in Israel and most of the rest in North America. Their history is long, their numbers have always been small, and their influence on how much of humanity thinks about God, law, justice and time is beyond calculation.

The story it tells about itself begins with Abraham, who left Mesopotamia at God’s call, and with his descendants, enslaved in Egypt and led out by Moses. At Mount Sinai the freed slaves entered a covenant: they would be God’s people and live by the Torah, the teaching. At its centre is the claim that there is one God, who cares how human beings treat each other. The prophets pressed the point: ritual without justice is worthless.

For a thousand years Jewish worship centred on the Temple in Jerusalem. The Romans destroyed it in the year 70 and scattered the people. What survived was a portable religion of study, prayer and practice built by the rabbis: the Mishnah, the Talmud, the synagogue, the Sabbath table. This rabbinic Judaism is the Judaism of today, carried through medieval Spain and Iraq, the villages of Poland and Yemen, and into the modern world.

It is a religion of action more than belief. The Torah contains 613 commandments, and the tradition has spent two thousand years working out how to keep them: what to eat, how to conduct business honestly, how to rest on the seventh day, how to mourn, how to give. It is also a religion of argument. Its central books are records of debate in which the minority view is preserved, and questioning is a form of devotion.

Modern Jews differ widely. The Orthodox keep traditional law closely. The Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist movements adapt it in various degrees. Many Jews are secular and express their identity through family, culture, memory and ethics. All share a calendar, a set of texts and a history that includes repeated persecution and the murder of six million European Jews between 1941 and 1945.

This Onda borrows practices that Jewish teachers readily share: waking with thanks, blessing food, studying with a partner, giving daily, taking stock at night and keeping a day of rest. Judaism does not seek converts, and holds that the righteous of all nations have a share in the world to come. You are a guest. The commandments particular to the covenant, and the Sabbath in its full form, belong to the Jewish people.

guide.era: Three thousand years and more, from the Israelite tribes to the present

figures.name: Moses
figures.bio: The prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Torah at Sinai. Called simply our teacher. He died within sight of the land he never entered.

figures.name: Hillel the Elder
figures.bio: A Babylonian-born sage in Jerusalem, famous for patience and for rulings that favoured ordinary people. His school’s views became the norm.

figures.name: Rabbi Akiva
figures.bio: A shepherd who began to study at forty and became the greatest scholar of his age. The Romans executed him for teaching Torah.

figures.name: Bruriah
figures.bio: A scholar of law quoted in the Talmud, whose rulings were accepted over those of leading rabbis. She taught her husband to pray for the end of sin, not of sinners.

figures.name: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki)
figures.bio: A winegrower of Troyes in France whose line-by-line commentaries on the Bible and Talmud are still printed beside the text and studied first.

figures.name: Maimonides (Rambam)
figures.bio: Born in Córdoba, physician to the sultan’s court in Cairo. He codified the whole of Jewish law and wrote the Guide for the Perplexed to reconcile it with philosophy.

figures.name: The Baal Shem Tov
figures.bio: A healer in the Carpathian foothills who taught that God is reached through joy, sincerity and song. Founder of Hasidism.

figures.name: Glückel of Hameln
figures.bio: A Hamburg merchant and mother of twelve whose memoirs, written for her children, are the first known autobiography by a Jewish woman.

figures.name: Abraham Joshua Heschel
figures.bio: A Polish-born rabbi and philosopher in America, who marched at Selma with Martin Luther King and said he felt his legs were praying.

figures.name: Regina Jonas
figures.bio: Ordained in Berlin in 1935, the first woman rabbi. She went on teaching and counselling in the Theresienstadt ghetto and was murdered at Auschwitz.

history.detail: An Egyptian inscription of about 1208 BCE is the first mention of a people called Israel. Tribes settle the hill country.
David makes Jerusalem his capital and Solomon builds the Temple. The kingdom splits. The prophets Amos, Isaiah and Jeremiah preach justice.
Nebuchadnezzar destroys Jerusalem and deports its leading families. In exile the scriptures are gathered and edited, and a religion takes shape that can live without a land.
Cyrus of Persia allows the exiles home. A new Temple is dedicated, and Ezra reads the Torah publicly.
A revolt against a Greek king who had banned Jewish practice ends with the rededication of the Temple, remembered at Hanukkah.
Rome crushes a Jewish revolt and burns the Temple. Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai founds a school at Yavneh, and study begins to take the place of sacrifice.
Rabbi Judah the Prince compiles the oral law. Three centuries of discussion of it in Babylonia are gathered into the Talmud.
Under Muslim rule in al-Andalus, Jewish poets, physicians and philosophers flourish. Maimonides is born at its end.
Crusaders destroy the Jewish communities of the Rhineland. In 1492 the Jews of Spain are forced to convert or leave, and settle around the Mediterranean and in the Ottoman empire.
The Baal Shem Tov’s movement of joyful piety sweeps Eastern Europe. In Berlin Moses Mendelssohn argues that Jews can be both observant and modern.
Jews gain citizenship across Western Europe. Reform, Conservative and modern Orthodox Judaism take shape. From 1881 pogroms in Russia drive two million to America.
Nazi Germany and its collaborators murder six million Jews, two thirds of the Jews of Europe, among them a million and a half children.
A Jewish state is declared in part of the ancient homeland, three years after the Shoah. Most Jews from Arab countries move there over the following decades.

concepts.detail: Made with Abraham, sealed at Sinai. It sets out obligations and promises on both sides and is understood to be permanent.
The five books are the written Torah. The oral Torah is the interpretation handed down with it, later written as the Mishnah and Talmud. Study never ends.
613 by the traditional count: 248 to do and 365 to refrain from. They cover ritual and ethics without distinguishing sharply between the two.
The tradition has two voices: legal reasoning about what to do, and story, parable and theology about why.
Thirty-nine kinds of creative work are set aside from Friday sunset. In their place come candles, wine, bread, song, study, sleep and company.
Human beings can always change course. The ten days from the New Year to the Day of Atonement are given to it, but the gates are said never to close.
The idea that Israel was singled out to keep the Torah. The tradition reads it as extra obligation, not superiority, and other peoples have their own paths.
The expectation of an age of peace and justice, when nation shall not lift up sword against nation. Views differ on whether a person or human effort will bring it.
All Jews are responsible for one another. Jewish identity is that of a people as well as of a faith, which is why a non-believing Jew remains a Jew.

facts.text: The Hebrew calendar counts from the traditional date of creation. The year that began in autumn 2026 is 5787.
A Torah scroll is written by hand with a quill on parchment, 304,805 letters in all. A single mistake makes it unfit until corrected.
The Talmud is printed with the same page layout in every edition. A reference such as Shabbat 31a will find the same words anywhere in the world.
Since 1923 Jews around the world have studied one page of Talmud a day in a shared cycle that takes about seven and a half years.
Hebrew ceased to be a daily spoken language for some seventeen centuries and was revived as a mother tongue at the end of the nineteenth.
The word chai, life, adds up to eighteen in Hebrew letters, so gifts to charity are often given in multiples of eighteen.

sensitivity.note: Judaism is the living tradition of a people. This Onda borrows practices of gratitude, study, giving and rest that Jewish teachers share openly. It is not a conversion course, and it does not ask you to take on commandments or symbols that belong to the covenant.
requiredCaveats: Jewish practice ranges from strictly Orthodox to secular. No single description fits everyone.
Antisemitism is old and present. If you meet stereotypes while exploring, name them for what they are.
Ritual objects such as the tallit, tefillin and Torah scroll are not for outsiders to use.
This Onda concerns the religion and its way of life. It takes no position on the politics of the modern Middle East.
